title: AI That Pays: Lessons from Revenue Cycle — Nathan Wan, Ensemble Health

primary.label: AI Product, UX & Human Factors
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 73%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk focuses on how AI products are deployed in healthcare RCM with human-in-the-loop workflows and measurable ROI, fitting the AI product and human-factors category. Revenue cycle management is an enterprise operations domain within healthcare life sciences. The talk covers deployed GenAI appeal systems in production and their measured outcomes. Requires familiarity with healthcare RCM and basic ML concepts but is accessible to a broad audience. The session is a conference talk from the AI Engineer channel. Multiple evidence anchors directly support the classification with transcript excerpts.

summary: Nathan Wan introduces Revenue Cycle Management (RCM) as an overlooked but critical domain within healthcare, noting that 40% of U.S. hospitals operate at negative margins—not from clinical costs but from broken, manual revenue cycle processes involving delays, denials, and lost revenue. Ensemble Health Partners, where Nathan heads AI, is an end-to-end RCM provider with approximately 14,000 employees serving hundreds of hospitals. Nathan shares his career path from Google (speech recognition, ambient documentation) through biotech startups (cancer diagnostics, microbiome drug discovery) before focusing on healthcare's administrative side, where ~20% of GDP is attributed to healthcare and administrative headcount has grown 30-fold over three decades while clinical headcount barely doubled. Friction between payers and providers drives significant cost, with denials as the largest component. Most denials are preventable technical errors, and payers are deploying AI to increase denial volumes, creating an arms race. Ensemble leverages longitudinal data to predict and correct denials before they happen, with prior authorization as a key use case. For clinical denials involving medical necessity disputes, GenAI accelerates appeal packet-building from EMRs that can be hundreds of pages long, containing text, images, labs, notes, and tables, alongside hundreds of clinical guidelines—all under tight deadlines. However, off-the-shelf GenAI models alone were insufficient; Ensemble worked directly with clinical experts to build a human-in-the-loop pipeline where experts make final quality decisions before submission. Results include a 40% reduction in processing time, higher quality measured by overturn rates, and increased volume—with ROI tracked concretely rather than hand-waved. Nathan acknowledges AI won't solve everything overnight given inconsistent rules, unstructured data, and systems scattered across platforms. Ensemble's EIQ platform unifies multiple data formats, though multimodal LLMs still face challenges parsing diverse EMR types. The team is building agents for all revenue cycle aspects, emphasizing that automation alone is insufficient—reasoning and connectivity are needed to fix errors upstream rather than just pushing processes faster. Ensemble's unique position combines the right data, team, and full RCM scope to intervene and act on behalf of clients.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and the Revenue Cycle Problem
sections.summary: Nathan introduces himself as Head of AI at Ensemble Health Partners, an end-to-end RCM organization with ~14,000 people serving hundreds of hospitals. He frames the problem: 40% of hospitals operate at negative margins due to broken, manual revenue cycle processes involving delays, denials, and lost revenue.

sections.title: Career Background: Google and Biotech
sections.summary: Nathan describes his career path: Google work on operational software, speech recognition, language modeling, and early ambient documentation; then biotech startups in cancer diagnostics from blood biomarkers and microbiome-based drug discovery. He contrasts these well-known AI-in-healthcare areas with the less flashy financial side.

sections.title: Healthcare's Financial Side: Scale and Complexity
sections.summary: He explains that ~20% of GDP goes to healthcare, with a large proportion being administrative. Administrative staff grew 30x over three decades while clinicians barely doubled. He defines key terminology: patients, providers, and payers including private insurance and government programs.

sections.title: Friction, Denials, and the Payer AI Arms Race
sections.summary: Friction between payers and providers drives significant cost, with denials as the largest component. A concrete claim example shows four denials, four appeals, and 200 days to payment. Payers are adopting AI to increase denial volumes. Most denials are technical errors, not medical disagreements, making them preventable.

sections.title: Ensemble's AI Approach: Prior Authorization and Clinical Denials
sections.summary: Ensemble's end-to-end view enables prediction and correction of denials before they happen. Prior authorization is a key use case. For clinical denials where medical necessity is disputed, GenAI can accelerate building appeal packets from patient records and care guidelines.

sections.title: Clinical Appeal Complexity and GenAI Approach
sections.summary: Nathan details the complexity of clinical appeals: EMRs are hundreds of pages with mixed data types (text, images, labs, notes, tables), hundreds of clinical guidelines apply differently across situations, and tight deadlines limit how many expert clinicians can participate. Off-the-shelf GenAI models alone were insufficient, so Ensemble built a human-in-the-loop pipeline where clinical experts make final quality decisions before letters are submitted to payers. Different service lines and clients add further complexity managed within the GenAI system.

sections.title: Measured Results and Direct ROI
sections.summary: Results include a 40% reduction in processing time (sometimes more), higher quality measured by overturn rates, and increased volume. Nathan emphasizes that ROI is tracked concretely and specifically, not hand-waved—a key advantage of applying AI to RCM with direct financial outcomes.

sections.title: Challenges, EIQ Platform, and Future Vision
sections.summary: Nathan acknowledges AI won't solve everything overnight given entrenched processes, inconsistent rules, unstructured data, and systems scattered across platforms. Ensemble's EIQ platform unifies multiple data formats, though multimodal LLMs still struggle with diverse EMR types. The team is building agents for all revenue cycle aspects, but automation alone is insufficient—reasoning and connectivity are needed to fix errors upstream. Ensemble's unique position combines the right data, team, and full RCM scope to lead this transformation.

demonstrations: Concrete claim example: a single claim denied four times, appealed four times, with provider receiving payment 200 days after the procedure, illustrating the cost of revenue cycle friction.
GenAI clinical appeal system with human-in-the-loop quality review by clinical experts, achieving 40% time reduction and higher overturn rates.
EIQ platform unifying multiple data formats across scattered systems into a single consistent infrastructure.
limitations: Off-the-shelf GenAI models alone were insufficient for generating quality appeal letters without expert collaboration
